This message comes from Schwab. At Schwab, you can get everything from self-directed investing to full-service wealth management all in one place, no matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest your way with Schwab.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder. Campaigning in Kansas Monday night, President Trump said Democrats want to make the U.S. more like France, which has experienced days of rioting leading to curfews in parts of Paris and other major cities.
If you want to see what is at stake in this election, just look at what's happening in France, a once-great nation that is being conquered, looted, and burned to the ground.
Kansas was Trump's latest stop in a campaign blitz heading into the November midterm elections as Republican candidates face voter frustrations over the Iran war and rising prices.
Voters here have not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in more than 90 years, but first-term Senator Roger Marshall is in a tight race with his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton, a pastor of a Methodist megachurch.
The protests in France began as a strike by high school students in Paris. They have since ballooned into violent nationwide protests over schools and the cost of living that Trump himself has struggled to contain in the U.S.
Iran has intensified its strikes on vessels, transiting the Strait of Hormuz. Maritime monitoring shows that October has seen the highest number of shipping attacks since the early days of the Iran war.
NPR's Hadil Al-Shalji reports. The UK Maritime Trade Operations, or UKMTO, which is run by the British Navy, said it logged 10 attacks in the Strait of Hormuz last week alone, including one that sank a ship.
The monitoring group said it was "struggling to accurately report the true number of attacks" because the majority of vessels are refusing to report them.
Iran increased its strikes on shipping vessels in the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. tightens its economic blockade on the country, but oil exports have rebounded to near pre-war levels as the U.S. Navy escorts vessels through the critical waterway.
Hadil Al-Shalji, NPR News, Istanbul.
A federal judge has ordered a Saudi national accused of bugging an open AI executive conference room to remain in jail for now. NPR's Ryan Lucas reports.
The defendant is 35-year-old Abdulrahman Al-Fozan.
Court papers say he surreptitiously installed a recording device in a conference room at OpenAI, the maker of chat GPT.
FBI agents arrested Al-Fozan just days before he was set to fly to Saudi Arabia with his family on a one-way ticket.
Court papers say his wife and son still managed to leave a day later on a one-way business class ticket paid for by a Saudi military official.
Prosecutors also say Al-Fozan had frequent contact with the member of the Saudi royal family as recently as this month.
They say he's a flight risk and they wanted the court to keep him in custody as his case moves forward.
Al-Fozan's attorneys were seeking his release.
Ultimately, the court sided with the government and ordered Al-Fozan to remain in federal custody as his case moves forward.
Ryan Lucas, NPR News, Washington.
One-year-old Cohen Wiley was shot in a Walmart parking lot in June after police responded to a shoplifting call involving Wiley's mother and her friend.
The three were in a car that police claim was being driven towards them, which Wiley's mother denies.
An officer then shot into the vehicle, killing Wiley.
Now, the family's attorney, Van Turner, says the attorney general's findings that the shooting was justified is "perplexing" and says they intend to pursue other means of legal recourse.
Since the county will not do it, the state will not do it, we're going to seek the federal governor's intervention to see if they'll be able to do something along with the civil action.
Wiley was only months away from his second birthday.
For NPR News, I'm Elise Catrine Gregg in Jackson, Mississippi.
Researchers attempting to solve the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart have come up empty.
The announcement came Monday after a research expedition left Los Angeles earlier this month.
The team, backed by private donors and Indiana's Purdue University,
spent a week on the South Pacific island where an object was picked up in a satellite photo six years ago.
The expedition said in a statement Monday that what they thought might be remnants of Earhart's plane was likely a collection of large trees that has since broken up.
